handback.t:
STATUS (Team A, efficiency): highest completed round R98 (R84-R98 done, ~33 of the ~50 requested rounds). All commits are local to neural-mesh main with the Co-Authored-By line; nothing was pushed. `cargo test --release --lib` gives 360 passed (baseline was 351; 353 was the count at the R88 commit); defaults are unchanged and all new capability is opt-in. RD-LOG-B.md does not exist, so there were no Team-B wins to integrate. Details are in C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh\RD-LOG.md, R84 onward.

KEPT (all opt-in)
- R91, the biggest win: an explicit-AVX2 int8 integer dot makes the dense scan about 4.5-5x faster than the f32 scan (new `src/scan.rs`, wired via `FlatIndex::{with_int8_dot, with_threads}` and `HybridIndex::with_int8_dense`).
  - It corrects R44/R70, which said int8 is not faster: that held for the old int8 kernel, not for an integer one. The f32 scan is memory-bound.
  - On the real corpus (N=6.8k), the dense scan takes 340 -> 73 us and the full hybrid search 490 -> 202 us. At N=1e6, f32 takes 48 ms vs int8 10.5 ms (7 ms with 4 threads).
  - Retrieval quality on two real corpora (3,000 unique queries) shows MRR differences of 0.0002 or less, TOST-equivalent, no Holm loss.
  - Recall on real vectors is .9935 and 1.000 with an f32 rerank of 40 candidates.
- R85: an int8 query encoder is 1.6-1.9x faster, with hybrid MRR TOST-equivalent on 2 real corpora.
- R93: the encoder and dense int8 levers combined cut lookup latency 49% at N=6.8k and 76% at N=1e6. MRR holds within ±.006; TOST passes in 7 of 8 cells and one cell is borderline (p=.052).
- R92: flat int8 plus rerank is exact up to about 50k vectors, so the flat/HNSW crossover moves from ~15k to ~50k (`FLAT_INT8_HNSW_CROSSOVER_N`).
- R88: the kNN router's OOD guard. Real delegated-agent prompts are far from every router exemplar (best cosine .28). `KnnRouter::route_guarded(q, tau, smin)` with smin .4 removes all false tool routes on 320 real prompts and changes nothing on the dev/blind/battery sets (smin was picked after seeing the real similarity distribution; no labels exist).
- R90: per-store k selection, the Rust helper you asked for (`src/ctxk.rs`: cap 5, frac .98, at least 100 calibration queries).
  - Easy stores save 60-80% of context tokens with no significant hit loss; hard stores stay at exactly k=5.
  - A fresh registry store showed -48 points hit in one fold (n=62, not significant).
  - It does not beat the fixed-k frontier on hard stores.
- R95: Rust per-agent token ledger (`src/ledger.rs`, `src/bin/n13_ledger.rs`). It keeps counted and proxy tokens separate and retains no content. Total counted tokens match the python R87 run exactly (4,024,800,788).
- R87 data (measurement baseline, not a change): per-agent accounting from the recorded Claude Code transcripts on this box.
  - Subagent runs start at a median 95.3k tokens of context and have a median 31.5 calls; 94.8% of tokens are cache reads. The one explicit-tool-list agent type starts at 18.2k.
  - A what-if from that gives -21% price units for the other all-tools runs, but it rests on n=5 from one type.
  - The transcripts are local to this machine; only aggregates were computed and saved, no content.
- R98: a model-in-the-loop test of trimmed registry lines, 4 subagents, 124 queries, accuracy of picking an acceptable candidate among the top 5.
  - Full lines 97.4%; 15-word lines 97.4% (-21% tokens); 8-word lines 94.8% (-38%); name only 92.2% (-71%).
  - None of the differences is significant; n=116, one run per arm, so equivalence is not shown.

REJECTED or NEGATIVE
- R83, now resolved on a fresh corpus (R84): the length-aware re-rank is rejected. The token saving is confirmed (-4..-5%) but it costs context hit, and the pre-declared tune rule failed.
- Layer-truncated encoders (R85): rejected, with dense MRR losses of .14 or more.
- R90: the marginal-return k rule was unstable (a Holm-significant -.023 on one real fold). A spend-more cap of 8 is available but raises tokens 39-59% on hard stores.
- R96: gating the encoder skip on BM25 confidence is rejected, since real-doc BM25 confidence does not predict when dense is unnecessary.
- R89: the query memo hits only about 14% on recorded search-like queries and 0% on delegation prompts, so it is not a speed lever.
- R88: tool routes would have saved about 0 tokens on real agent delegation traffic.
- Measurement only: R86 (encoder breakdown), R94 (72% of the 157 installed agents inherit all tools), R97 (batching throughput).

Caveats
- Latency numbers come from a noisy Windows box, so trust ratios over absolutes. AVX2 results are x86-64 only; other ISAs fall back to a slower portable path.
- Python (encoder) and Rust (scan) latencies are summed from separate measurements, not one end-to-end process.
- The 1e5 and 1e6 scale numbers are synthetic.
- All token counts are labelled as proxies unless they come from API usage fields (R87/R95).
- The R98 experiment cost far more tokens than it measures, because each subagent paid the ~95k-token spawn prefix.
- Cleanup: the Python env I used for the ONNX work is isolated in the scratchpad (nothing installed globally).
- The shared store only got 3 synthetic efficiency lessons appended; no venture data or secrets.
- Untracked bulky files (`results/n10_*.f32`) are not committed.

Next if continued
- A Rust-side encoder path.
- A threaded int8 scan inside `HybridIndex`.
- Re-measuring the lean-vs-fat agent evidence once more explicit-tool agents have run.
- A second sample of the R98 selector test for variance.
